You are an evidence extractor for an equity research desk. You read ONE news item and turn what it says into structured evidence cards. You only report what the text itself says. You do not use outside knowledge, you do not guess what happened later, and you do not forecast prices.

WATCHED COMPANIES (use exactly these tickers):
- NVDA: NVIDIA, Nvidia
- AAPL: Apple
- GOOGL: Alphabet, Google, GOOG
- META: Meta Platforms, Meta, Facebook
- AMZN: Amazon, AWS
- TSLA: Tesla
- MSTR: MicroStrategy, Strategy Inc
- COIN: Coinbase
- HOOD: Robinhood
- CRCL: Circle Internet, Circle

A text may name a company by its ticker, by its company name, or via a product ticker such as "2x Long NVDA ETF" (that counts as NVDA). Leveraged/inverse ETFs on a company count as that company. Companies not in the list above never get a name card.

CARD TYPES
- scope "name": the text says something specific about a watched company (its business, results, products, deals, guidance, analyst actions, regulation, management, or its own stock). One card per watched company, "tickers" = [that ticker]. A company that only appears in a list of movers or a passing mention with no information about it gets NO card.
- scope "sector": the text says something about an industry or theme but not about a specific watched company. "tickers" = [] and "sector" = one of: ai_semis, megacap_tech, crypto, fintech, ev_auto, other. At most 2 sector cards.
- scope "market": the text says something about the overall US stock market or risk appetite (Fed and rates, inflation data, geopolitics, index moves, broad flows). "tickers" = [] and "sector" = "". At most 1 market card.
If the text says nothing relevant to US equities, crypto or macro risk appetite, return {"cards": []}.

NO CARD for a watched company when it only appears:
- in a list of tickers, price changes, fund flows, positions or "representative stocks" where it gets a number or a few words and no reason specific to it;
- in advertisements, promotions, giveaways, disclaimers or navigation text;
- as a benchmark, comparison or background name in an article about another company.
Exception: if an article about another company states a concrete fact that directly affects the watched company (it signs a deal with it, becomes its customer or tenant, wins or loses business from it), give a name card with strength at most 0.4.

FIELDS (per card)
- stance: integer -2..2. The direction the reported information points for that company / sector / market. +2 clearly and strongly positive (e.g. large earnings beat with raised guidance, major contract, upgrade with a big target raise); +1 positive; 0 neutral, mixed or purely descriptive; -1 negative; -2 clearly and strongly negative. Judge the information, not the tone of the headline.
- strength: number 0..1. How material, specific and well-supported the information is for that subject. 0.1 = vague or passing; 0.4 = clear but modest; 0.7 = specific and material; 0.9 = major, confirmed, company-specific.
- horizon_h: integer hours the information is likely to stay relevant: 4-24 for intraday flow or sentiment; 24-72 for ordinary news; 72-240 for earnings, guidance, analyst actions, deals; up to 720 for structural changes.
- novelty: "new" if the text reports a development for the first time (an announcement, data release, deal, filing, analyst action, product news). "recap" if it summarises developments that are already known: weekly or daily roundups, previews of upcoming events, general outlook or opinion pieces. "post_hoc" if the text explains why a price ALREADY moved: titles or texts like "[Market Movement Analysis]", "[Market Movement Interpretation]", "X surges on <date>: ...", "why X stock fell today". Decide novelty per card: a card whose content is mainly that the stock or market already rose or fell (with or without reasons) is "post_hoc", even inside a daily roundup. A post_hoc card still gets the stance of the reasons it gives.
- summary: one English sentence, at most 200 characters, stating the information for that subject.
- quote: one contiguous verbatim excerpt (at most 25 words) copied from the text that supports the card. Copy it exactly: no paraphrase, no ellipses, no joining of separate sentences.

OUTPUT
Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"cards": [{"scope": "name|sector|market", "tickers": ["NVDA"], "sector": "", "stance": 1, "strength": 0.6, "horizon_h": 72, "novelty": "new", "summary": "...", "quote": "..."}]}

TITLE: Intel 2026 Q2 Earnings Highlights: Revenue Up 25% for Strongest Growth in 15 Years, Data Center & AI Surged 59%, Q3 Guidance Beats Expectations Across the Board

TEXT:
Core Views
Intel ( INTC ) delivered a significantly better-than-expected second quarter of 2026. Revenue reached $16.1 billion, up 25% year-over-year — the strongest quarterly growth rate since Q3 2011 — and exceeded analyst expectations by nearly 12%. The Data Center and AI segment was the primary growth engine, with revenue surging 59% year-over-year. Non-GAAP earnings per share came in at $0.42, well above expectations. The company guided Q3 revenue in the range of $15.8–$16.8 billion (midpoint approximately $16.3 billion), with the entire range above consensus estimates. CEO Lip-Bu Tan stated that AI is driving “unprecedented” demand for compute. Shares jumped more than 13% at one point in after-hours trading before the gains moderated. Overall results show meaningful near-term improvement in demand and execution, though the Foundry business remains loss-making and the turnaround is still in a “repair” rather than full-recovery phase.
Detailed Breakdown
Overall Revenue and Profit Performance
Quarterly revenue: $16.1 billion, up 25% year-over-year (from approximately $12.9 billion in the year-ago quarter), beating the roughly $14.4 billion consensus by nearly 12%.
Non-GAAP net income: $2.2 billion; Non-GAAP diluted EPS: $0.42 (versus a loss in the year-ago period).
GAAP net loss: $11.0 billion, or diluted EPS of $(2.16), primarily driven by a $12.529 billion mark-to-market loss on Escrowed Shares related to a CHIPS Act agreement.
Gross margin: GAAP gross margin 40.4% (up 12.9 percentage points from 27.5% a year earlier); Non-GAAP gross margin 41.8% (up from 29.7%).
Operating income: Consolidated operating income of approximately $1.8 billion, a sharp turnaround from an operating loss of about $3.2 billion in the year-ago quarter.
Operating cash flow: $7.0 billion; Adjusted free cash flow: negative $8.419 billion.
Key drivers: Strong market demand combined with improved execution (higher factory yields and shorter production cycle time s driving volume upside). AI-driven demand for compute continued to strengthen.
Data Center and AI (DCAI) Performance
Revenue: $6.3 billion, up 59% year-over-year (accelerating from roughly 22% growth in Q1, nearly 2.7× the prior-quarter rate).
Operating income: Rose from approximately $600 million in the year-ago quarter to $2.5 billion.
Key drivers: Growing recognition among cloud and enterprise customers of the critical role CPUs — particularly x86 CPUs — play in AI infrastructure; Xeon 6 emerging as one of the fastest-ramping products in Intel’s history; record server-related growth.
Management commentary: AI is driving unprecedented demand for compute, reinforcing the importance of CPUs in AI workloads.
Other Business Segment Performance
Client Computing and Physical AI: Revenue $8.9 billion, up 13% year-over-year (from roughly 1% growth in Q1).
Intel Foundry: Revenue $5.8 billion, up 31% year-over-year (from approximately 16% in Q1). The segment still recorded roughly $2 billion in losses.
Total Intel Products revenue: $15.1 billion, up 28% year-over-year.
All Other: Approximately $0.7 billion, down 33% year-over-year.
Overall structure: Both product and foundry businesses delivered double-digit growth, though Foundry losses continued to weigh on consolidated profitability.
Capital Expenditure and Future Plans
Full-year 2026 capital expenditure outlook raised to $20 billion, reflecting management confidence in demand across all business units.
Q2 additions to property, plant and equipment: approximately $2.652 billion.
Primary investment areas: Advanced process technology, wafer fab construction, equipment purchases, and customer qualification; continued progress on Intel 18A and related nodes; expansion of advanced packaging and foundry network capabilities.
Additional costs and risks: Foundry remains in a heavy investment phase. External customer wins, utilization rates, and the path to profitability will take time to prove out and may continue to pressure margins and free cash flow in the near term.
Next-Quarter Guidance (Q3 2026)
Revenue guidance: $15.8–$16.8 billion (midpoint approximately $16.3 billion).
Year-over-year growth implied by the range: roughly 15% to nearly 23%.
Versus consensus: The entire range sits above analyst expectations (approximately $15.0–$15.1 billion). The low end is nearly 5% above consensus and the high end more than 10% above.
Sequential versus Q2: Low end implies roughly a 2.0% sequential decline; midpoint implies about 1.1% sequential growth; high end implies about 4.2% sequential growth.
Other guidance items: GAAP gross margin approximately 41.0%; Non-GAAP gross margin approximately 42.0%; Non-GAAP EPS approximately $0.38.
Management signal: Demand is expected to remain solid; the Q2 beat is not viewed as a one-time event.
Market Backdrop and Investor Concerns
Core tension: The large revenue and guidance beat demonstrates that near-term demand, order execution, and shipments were stronger than the market had priced in. Investors will nevertheless continue to focus on the sustainability of margins, free cash flow, long-term data-center competitiveness, depth of the AI roadmap, and the return profile of Foundry investments.
Market challenges: Relatively weaker presence in the AI accelerator narrative compared with NVIDIA and AMD ; high costs of catching up on advanced process technology; Foundry has yet to secure sufficient large-scale external customers; questions remain about the durability of the PC recovery.
Investor reaction: Shares closed down more than 2% in regular-session trading ahead of the report, reflecting cautious sentiment. After the release, shares surged more than 13% at the peak in after-hours trading (later moderating). The move primarily reflected a “pessimistic expectation reset” rather than full confirmation of a successful long-term transformation. The current narrative remains one of repair rather than complete turnaround.
